title: Lymphatic Drainage
subject: Immune and Lymphatic System (IMMU)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows lymph from the tissues to the veins of the neck. It traces the cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, and right lymphatic duct, maps the territory of each palpable node group, and applies that map to infections, first nodal spread of tumors, the Virchow node, and chylothorax. Board questions usually describe an enlarged node or a tumor site and ask where the problem started or where it will spread first. Two rules carry most of these questions: skin and body wall drain to the nearest superficial node group, while an organ drains along its arteries back to the place where it developed.

sections.title: The two main ducts and their territories

blocks.text: Lymphatic capillaries collect the fluid and plasma protein that capillaries filter but do not reabsorb. Valved collecting vessels carry this lymph through chains of nodes to a few large trunks and then to two ducts that empty into the great veins of the neck, returning about 2 to 3 L to the blood each day (the forces that move it are covered in IM-9).
Lower body and abdomen: the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct

Lymph from the lower limbs and pelvis passes through iliac nodes to the lumbar (lateral aortic) nodes and forms the right and left lumbar trunks. Lymph from the gut passes through preaortic nodes (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric) into the intestinal trunk. These trunks join at the cisterna chyli, which lies in front of the L1 to L2 vertebral bodies, between the aorta and the right crus of the diaphragm.

The thoracic duct leaves the cisterna chyli and enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus at about T12. In the lower posterior mediastinum it lies to the right of the midline, behind the esophagus, between the thoracic aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. At about T4 to T6 it crosses to the left, ascends along the left side of the esophagus into the root of the neck, arches laterally at about C7, and empties into the left venous angle, the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. Near its end it usually receives the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks, so it drains the left side of the head, neck, upper limb, and thorax as well as everything below the diaphragm.

blocks.text: The right upper quarter: the right lymphatic duct

The right jugular, right subclavian, and right bronchomediastinal trunks drain the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right side of the thorax. They may join as a short right lymphatic duct, about 1 cm long, or open separately into the right venous angle.

blocks.text: The thoracic duct also carries chyle. Chylomicrons formed from long-chain fat in enterocytes are too large to enter villous blood capillaries, so they enter the central lacteal of each villus and reach the blood through the thoracic duct rather than the portal vein. Thoracic duct lymph is therefore milky after a fatty meal and clear during fasting.

blocks.predict: A tumor encases the cisterna chyli. Which body regions would develop lymphedema, and would fat absorption change?
blocks.explain: Both lower limbs, the pelvis, and the genitalia lose their outflow, and chylomicrons cannot leave the gut, so chylous ascites and fat malabsorption follow. The upper limbs and head drain normally because their trunks join the ducts in the neck.

sections.title: Palpable node groups and their territories

blocks.text: Afferent lymph carries microbes, antigen, and tumor cells to the subcapsular sinus of the first node it reaches. When a node meets antigen it enlarges: lymphocytes proliferate in follicles (B cells) or the paracortex (T cells), macrophages fill the sinuses, and inflammation adds edema. Rapid swelling stretches the capsule, so infected nodes are usually tender, whereas tumor infiltration enlarges a node slowly and with fibrosis, making it hard, nontender, and fixed to surrounding tissue. Lymphoma typically produces firm, rubbery nodes. Localized enlargement points to the drainage territory; enlargement in two or more noncontiguous regions (generalized lymphadenopathy) points to a systemic process such as infectious mononucleosis, HIV infection, secondary syphilis, systemic lupus erythematosus, lymphoma, or leukemia.

Superficial lymph vessels tend to run with superficial veins, which explains the less obvious territories. The epitrochlear (cubital) nodes lie above the medial epicondyle beside the basilic vein and receive lymph from the ulnar side of the hand and forearm, while radial-side vessels follow the cephalic vein directly to axillary nodes. Skin and superficial tissue below the umbilicus drain to the superficial inguinal nodes, and above the umbilicus to the axillary nodes. The vertical group of superficial inguinal nodes follows the great saphenous vein and drains most of the lower limb skin, but the lateral foot and back of the calf follow the small saphenous vein to the popliteal nodes.

blocks.text: Normal nodes are usually under about 1 cm, though inguinal nodes up to about 1.5 to 2 cm are common in adults because the legs and feet are exposed to constant minor injury. Any palpable supraclavicular node is abnormal and carries a high likelihood of malignancy, because the supraclavicular nodes drain the chest and abdomen rather than exposed skin. Some exceptions in the inguinal territory are worth knowing: the glans penis and glans clitoris drain to deep inguinal and external iliac nodes, and lymph from the uterine fundus near the attachment of the round ligament can follow the ligament to the superficial inguinal nodes.

Tender, warm node suggests infection; hard, fixed suggests tumor

blocks.text: Carcinomas typically spread first through lymphatics, so the first nodes involved can be predicted from the drainage map. Two rules decide nearly every question. Skin, and any surface lined by skin, drains to the nearest superficial node group. An organ drains along its arteries back toward the aorta, to nodes at the level where its arteries arise, which reflects where the organ developed rather than where it ends up.
Breast

About three quarters of breast lymph, including nearly all from the lateral quadrants, drains to the axillary nodes, first to the pectoral (anterior) group and then through central and apical groups to the subclavian trunk. Most of the rest, mainly from the medial quadrants, follows perforating branches of the internal thoracic vessels to the parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes beside the sternum. Some lymph from the inferior quadrants reaches abdominal nodes, and some crosses to the opposite breast. Carcinoma is most common in the upper outer quadrant, which contains the most glandular tissue, so axillary nodes are the usual first site of spread; a medial tumor can involve parasternal nodes that are not palpable.
Testis and scrotum

The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidney and descends through the inguinal canal, bringing its testicular artery from the aorta at about L2 and its lymphatics with it. Testicular lymph therefore runs in the spermatic cord to the lumbar (para-aortic and paracaval) nodes near the renal vessels, so testicular cancer spreads first to the retroperitoneum, not the groin. The scrotum is skin of the body wall and drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. The ovary follows the same rule as the testis and drains to para-aortic nodes.
Anal canal and the pectinate line

The pectinate line marks where the endoderm-derived hindgut meets the ectoderm-derived proctodeum, and arteries, veins, nerves, and lymph all change there. Above the line the canal is supplied by the superior rectal artery and lined by columnar epithelium, and its lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes. Below the line it is supplied by the inferior rectal artery, lined by stratified squamous epithelium, and drains with the perineal skin to the superficial inguinal nodes.

blocks.title: Worked example: testis versus scrotum
blocks.text: A 28-year-old man has a firm, painless testicular mass, and a 70-year-old former chimney sweep has an ulcerated scrotal lesion. Which nodes are checked first in each? Step 1: the testis is an organ that formed near the kidney, and its artery arises from the aorta at about L2. Step 2: its lymph follows that artery, so the first nodes are para-aortic, imaged in the retroperitoneum, and groin nodes are normally spared. Step 3: the scrotal lesion is squamous carcinoma of skin, and scrotal skin is body wall below the umbilicus. Step 4: its first nodes are superficial inguinal, which can be palpated. An enlarged inguinal node in a man with testicular cancer suggests scrotal involvement or altered drainage, not the usual route.

The left supraclavicular nodes lie beside the termination of the thoracic duct at the left venous angle. They are the last nodes on the path of lymph from the abdomen, pelvis, lower limbs, and left thorax before it enters the blood. An enlarged, hard, nontender left supraclavicular node is called the Virchow node, and finding it on examination is the Troisier sign. It is classically associated with gastric adenocarcinoma but occurs with many abdominal, pelvic, and thoracic cancers and with lymphoma.

Two mechanisms carry tumor cells there. Tumor cells that enter the abdominal lymphatics pass through, or bypass, regional preaortic and para-aortic nodes, travel up the thoracic duct, and lodge in nodes at its terminal portion. In addition, when tumor obstructs the end of the duct, lymph backs up and flows retrogradely into the neighboring supraclavicular nodes, carrying tumor cells with it. Either way, a node in the neck can be the first palpable sign of a cancer that is hidden in the abdomen and has already spread beyond its regional nodes, which is why the finding implies advanced disease.

Cells ascend the thoracic duct
Cells lodge in nodes at the left venous angle

blocks.caption: Abdominal lymph reaches only the left venous angle, so abdominal cancer produces a left, not a right, supraclavicular node.

blocks.text: The side matters. The right supraclavicular nodes drain the right upper quarter, including the mediastinum, lungs, and esophagus, but receive no abdominal lymph, so a hard right supraclavicular node points to lung or esophageal cancer or lymphoma rather than an abdominal primary. The left supraclavicular nodes can also enlarge from left lung or mediastinal disease, because the left bronchomediastinal trunk joins the end of the thoracic duct. A Virchow node is distinguished from a reactive node by its features: reactive nodes from upper limb or neck infection are tender and mobile, whereas metastatic nodes are hard, nontender, and often matted or fixed because tumor provokes a fibrous (desmoplastic) reaction.

blocks.predict: A 66-year-old with weight loss and early satiety has a hard 2 cm node above the right clavicle and none on the left. Is gastric cancer the most likely source?
blocks.explain: No. The stomach drains through the thoracic duct to the left venous angle. A right supraclavicular node reflects the right lymphatic territory, so the mediastinum, lung, or esophagus is the likelier source, and weight loss with early satiety can accompany an esophageal or mediastinal cancer.

blocks.text: A chylothorax is chyle in the pleural space. It follows disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct or its tributaries. The leading causes are surgical injury (esophagectomy, lung resection, and other cardiothoracic or neck operations) and malignancy, of which lymphoma is the most frequent nontraumatic cause; chest trauma and venous thrombosis that raises pressure at the venous angle also cause it. Because a resting adult sends about 1.5 to 2.5 L of lymph through the duct each day, and more after fatty meals, a torn duct can fill a hemithorax quickly.
Which side?

The side follows the course of the duct. Below about T5 the duct lies right of midline in the posterior mediastinum, so injury there usually produces a right chylothorax. Above the crossing it lies on the left, so injury there, as in surgery at the left root of the neck or upper mediastinum, usually produces a left chylothorax. Injury near the crossing or mediastinal leakage can produce bilateral effusions.

Milky, triglyceride-rich, lymphocyte-predominant fluid accumulates

blocks.caption: Volume rises when enteral fat is given, because fat increases intestinal lymph flow.

blocks.text: The fluid explained

Each finding in the fluid follows from what the duct carries. Chylomicrons scatter light, so the fluid is milky white and stays milky after centrifugation, unlike an empyema, whose turbidity comes from cells and clears when they are spun down. Chylomicrons are triglyceride-rich, so pleural triglyceride above about 110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L) strongly supports chylothorax, a value below about 50 mg/dL (0.56 mmol/L) makes it unlikely, and lipoprotein analysis showing chylomicrons confirms it. The duct carries recirculating lymphocytes, mainly T cells, so the cells are predominantly lymphocytes. Chyle has little ability to irritate the pleura, so the fluid is usually odorless and the effusion can be large without fever or much pain.

blocks.title: Milky pleural fluid: chylothorax versus pseudochylothorax
rows: Long-standing effusion with thickened pleura (tuberculosis, rheumatoid pleurisy)
Days after injury or with a new tumor
blocks.caption: Milkiness alone does not identify chyle; chylomicrons and the triglyceride level do.

blocks.text: A fasting patient is an important exception. When no fat is being absorbed, chyle contains few chylomicrons and can look clear or serous, so a postoperative patient kept without food may show a nonmilky effusion that turns milky once enteral feeding resumes. Medium-chain fatty acids are absorbed directly into portal blood bound to albumin and are not packaged into chylomicrons, which is why they add little to chyle flow. Prolonged leakage depletes what the duct carries: fat and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), protein (hypoalbuminemia and low immunoglobulins), and lymphocytes (lymphopenia), producing malnutrition and impaired immunity. Leakage into the peritoneum causes chylous ascites, and in lymphatic filariasis abnormal lymph-urinary connections cause chyluria.

blocks.title: Worked example: predicting the side and the fluid
blocks.text: Four days after an esophagectomy with an incision through the right chest, a patient who has just started enteral feeding develops a large right pleural effusion. Step 1: the lower thoracic duct lies right of midline beside the esophagus, below its crossing at about T5, so injury during the dissection gives a right effusion. Step 2: the delay fits feeding, which raised chyle flow and made the fluid milky. Step 3: expect milky fluid that stays milky after centrifugation, triglyceride above about 110 mg/dL, chylomicrons, and lymphocyte predominance. Step 4: if drainage continues, expect falling albumin, falling lymphocyte count, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

integration.text: Embryology explains both the drainage map and its variants. The thoracic duct forms from paired embryonic lymph channels that anastomose, with the lower part of the right channel, the anastomosis, and the upper part of the left persisting, which is why the adult duct rises on the right and ends on the left, and why duplicated or right-sided terminations occur. The gonads and their vessels descend from the posterior abdominal wall, and the pectinate line marks the meeting of endoderm and ectoderm, so the same embryology that sets blood and nerve supply also sets lymph drainage.

Immunology and pathology explain what the map predicts. Regional nodes filter afferent lymph, so an enlarged node is a reactive or infiltrated node in the territory of an infection or tumor; carcinomas characteristically spread through lymphatics, whereas sarcomas more often spread through the blood, so the map applies best to carcinomas. Its limits are real: drainage varies between people, tumors can skip the first node, and obstructed lymphatics reroute flow, so a predicted first node is a probability, not a certainty. The thoracic duct also links nutrition, fluid balance, and immunity, which is why its injury affects all three.

summary: Lymph from the lower limbs, pelvis, and gut collects in the cisterna chyli at L1 to L2 and ascends the thoracic duct through the aortic hiatus.
The thoracic duct runs right of midline in the lower posterior mediastinum, crosses to the left at about T4 to T6, and empties at the left venous angle.
The right lymphatic duct, or its separate trunks, drains only the right head and neck, right upper limb, and right thorax.
Skin and body wall drain to the nearest superficial node group; below the umbilicus that is the superficial inguinal group.
Epitrochlear nodes drain the ulnar side of the hand and forearm; popliteal nodes drain the lateral foot and back of the leg.
Organs drain along their arteries to where they developed: testis and ovary to para-aortic nodes, scrotum to superficial inguinal nodes.
Lateral breast drains to axillary nodes and medial breast to parasternal nodes; the anal canal drains to internal iliac nodes above the pectinate line and superficial inguinal nodes below it.
A hard left supraclavicular (Virchow) node signals abdominal or thoracic cancer carried up the thoracic duct, classically gastric adenocarcinoma; a right one points to the chest.
Thoracic duct injury below about T5 causes a right chylothorax and above it a left one; the fluid is milky, triglyceride above about 110 mg/dL, with chylomicrons and lymphocytes.
Pseudochylothorax is cholesterol-rich and lacks chylomicrons; prolonged chyle loss causes malnutrition, fat-soluble vitamin loss, and lymphopenia.

The pleural triglyceride thresholds (above about 110 mg/dL supportive, below about 50 mg/dL against) and cholesterol cutoff of about 200 mg/dL for pseudochylothorax follow common clinical consensus; some sources use slightly different values.
Daily lymph and thoracic duct flow (about 2 to 3 L total, about 1.5 to 2.5 L through the duct) are approximate and vary with fat intake and source.
Normal node size limits (about 1 cm, inguinal up to about 1.5 to 2 cm) are approximate clinical conventions, not fixed standards.
The proportion of breast lymph draining to axillary nodes (about 75%) follows Moore; other texts quote similar but not identical figures.
